claims.text: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Untreated NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
Untreated NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical performance at approximately 1600 °C.
Untreated NbMoTaW has predicted irradiation resistance.
Adding about 5 at% Ti to NbMoTaW will produce nanoscale Ti-rich second-phase precipitates.
The Ti-rich precipitates will be uniformly dispersed within the BCC matrix.
A refractory BCC alloy containing 5 at% Ti can retain a single-phase BCC structure.
Ti-rich precipitates will reduce the local Peierls barrier and resistance to dislocation motion at room temperature.
Ti-rich precipitates will act as dislocation-nucleation sites and promote stress relief.
The Ti addition will significantly increase room-temperature tensile elongation relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
The Ti addition will lower room-temperature yield strength relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
The Ti-doped alloy will maintain mechanical performance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW at approximately 1600 °C.
The Ti-doped alloy will retain irradiation resistance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW.
Overall lattice distortion underpins both the high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW.
Adding about 5 at% Ti will preserve the lattice distortion responsible for high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
The nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates will remain stable without coarsening across room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation conditions.
Keeping the Ti content near 5 at% will avoid large, continuous, or brittle precipitates that compromise the BCC structure.
Ti-containing single-phase BCC Zr-Nb-Ti medium-entropy alloys can exhibit room-temperature elongation above 10% and negligible irradiation hardening.
Sequential Kr and He irradiation is similar to the irradiation treatment used in the cited prior work.

contradictions.description: The intervention and mediator require Ti-rich second-phase particles, whereas the experiment says both doped and undoped samples should be ensured to have a single-phase BCC structure. A distinct second phase is incompatible with a strictly single-phase specification unless the particles are merely compositional fluctuations within the same BCC phase.
